criteria.label: Game design
criteria.description: Playability, fairness, feedback, pacing, visual readability, and how the mall and store mechanics work together.

criteria.label: Code architecture
criteria.description: Separation of rules and presentation, state ownership, determinism, module boundaries, and integration between systems.

criteria.label: Code design
criteria.description: Algorithms, data models, APIs, collision and input handling, correctness, and how easily the implementation can be extended.

criteria.label: Code cleanliness
criteria.description: Readability, naming, formatting, duplication, useful comments, type discipline, and removal of unfinished or disconnected code.

criteria.label: Prompt completeness
criteria.description: Working coverage of the original prompt: traversal, packages, stores, enemies, extras, power-ups, screens, audio, art, input, and technical constraints.

implementations.name: Claude Sonnet 5.5
implementations.note: The most convincing mall: rich art, fair encounters, and broad coverage. Strong rule boundaries; the store module is oversized.

assessment.gameDesign: Detailed storefronts, lively characters, themed rooms, and clear search feedback make the caper feel coherent. Entry protection and guard delays improve fairness. Busy patterns and a dense HUD sometimes compete with the action.
assessment.architecture: A frame-driven Session owns the game flow; seeded rules and typed events are separated from browser, audio, and drawing. The boundaries are consistently exercised in Node. Some presentation state lives in the overlay rather than the simulation.
assessment.codeDesign: Input preserves printed-letter layouts and repeated taps; store movement, collision, searching, and guard behavior share explicit models. The roughly 1,200-line store module concentrates too many responsibilities despite otherwise focused modules.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict TypeScript, clear contracts, useful comments, and descriptive behavior tests make the implementation easy to follow. A few large modules and dense rendering code reduce local readability.
assessment.completeness: Very broad coverage of traversal, store extras, power-ups, generated art and music, and session screens. Its 477 tests include long seeded simulation runs. Sampled title, arrival, and store entry worked; this review did not establish a complete uninterrupted playthrough.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed

implementations.name: Claude Fable 5.1
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: Colorful, generous, and feature-rich, with dependable seeded rules. Large mall and store modules and busy floors limit polish.

assessment.gameDesign: Distinct stores, strong feedback, generous entry protection, and considerate search controls support the exploration loop. The busy floor patterns and compact HUD reduce readability in otherwise attractive scenes.
assessment.architecture: Pure frame-based game modules emit typed events to a separate renderer and audio layer. State and seeded setup are explicit. Type-only references to art and audio identities introduce mild coupling, and the mall module remains large.
assessment.codeDesign: Connected room layouts, accessible fixtures, corner assistance, and explicit interaction rules are thoughtfully implemented. The roughly 1,350-line mall and 650-line store modules would benefit from smaller responsibility boundaries.
assessment.cleanliness: Consistent strict TypeScript and readable names make the rules approachable. Comments explain deliberate gameplay choices. Long rule files and occasional tightly packed branches add maintenance cost.
assessment.completeness: The broad prompt coverage includes store-specific jokes, traversal, loot, powers, generated graphics, and sound. All 321 tests and the typechecked build passed. Browser sampling confirmed a real store transition and package search after preparing the player's position.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall, prepared store entry and package collection passed

implementations.name: Claude Opus 5
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, indexed framebuffer & WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A thorough, playable caper with strong palette rules and safety fixes. Huge rule files and injected callbacks complicate maintenance.

assessment.gameDesign: The mall and themed stores feel substantial, with useful feedback and safeguards against unavoidable spawn and ambush deaths. The detailed art is undermined slightly by busy backgrounds and a cramped HUD.
assessment.architecture: A pure core communicates through a typed EventBus; rendering and audio read state. Seeded frame timing and structural palette limits are strong choices. Globally injected transition callbacks and very large mall/store modules weaken isolation.
assessment.codeDesign: Collision, floor geometry, fixture reachability, elevator latches, and emergence grace receive careful treatment and regression coverage. The callback wiring and roughly 1,800-line mall module make extensions harder than the underlying models require.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict typing, centralized constants and copy, and comments explaining design decisions keep the implementation consistent. Long functions and files make it harder to trace a single interaction through the rules.
assessment.completeness: Extensive coverage of the game loop, store extras, powers, generated assets, and CRT requirements. All 217 tests and the typechecked build passed. Sampled title, mall, and prepared store entry worked; full-route completion was not independently replayed here.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed

implementations.name: Claude Opus 5.5
implementations.note: Rich arcade detail and focused rule modules. Pixi scenes own some scoring and timing, and busy rooms weaken visual clarity.

assessment.gameDesign: Recognizable characters, themed storefronts, and broad arcade interactions create an engaging world. Striped rooms and large speech text can obscure the action; the presentation is less legible than its feature coverage suggests.
assessment.architecture: Physics, elevators, combat, and store worlds have useful rule modules. However, Pixi scenes also own scoring, transition timing, and presentation state; mutable global store hooks introduce initialization dependencies. The pure boundary is incomplete.
assessment.codeDesign: Focused world updates, seeded content, and queued layout-aware input are good foundations. Scene-owned state and fixed store placement make independent simulation and larger-room extensions less straightforward.
assessment.cleanliness: Most modules are short, sensibly named, and supported by behavior tests. Task-number comments and scene/world overlap add noise, and untyped shared hooks provide weaker contracts than the strongest TypeScript entries.
assessment.completeness: A broad implementation with many mechanics, generated sprites and sounds, and a working sampled store transition. All 319 tests and the production build passed; a sizable portion of the suite validates assets. Scene coupling and room-camera limitations leave technical prompt gaps.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed

implementations.name: GPT-6.1 Sol
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D & WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A compact, broadly working game with useful route tests. One large rules file, simpler art, and uneven encounter protection hold it back.

assessment.gameDesign: Readable characters, clear package feedback, and functional movement support a convincing core loop. Store decoration is comparatively sparse, first-visit interruptions freeze the player, and ambush protection is less considerate than in the strongest entries.
assessment.architecture: The rules are pure and seeded, with separate drawing, input, and audio. A roughly 1,650-line game file owns most systems, and string events plus shared actor collections blur subsystem boundaries.
assessment.codeDesign: BFS navigation, fixture geometry, corner assistance, and explicit search controls are solid. A very broad Game state, short variable names, shared mall/store actors, and UI-string power identities make the model harder to extend.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict typing, a small dependency footprint, and useful verification documentation are strengths. Large files and compressed branches reduce readability, though the code is substantially clearer than the earlier Sol implementation.
assessment.completeness: Most gameplay systems, extras, powers, and generated audio are represented. All 75 tests and the typechecked build passed. Browser sampling confirmed prepared store entry and package collection. Art detail and some encounter behavior fall short of the most complete implementations.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall, prepared store entry and package collection passed

implementations.name: Claude Opus 4.6
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D with CRT effect, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A substantial core, but several features stop at emitted events. Simplified collisions, mismatched audio hooks, and dark art hurt play.

assessment.gameDesign: The sampled title, mall, and store transition work, and many arcade systems are present. Dark sprites, simplified room interactions, missing visible dialogue, and inconsistent hazard handling make the experience less convincing.
assessment.architecture: Seeded rules, event output, and separate rendering/audio form a sound outline. The roughly 2,500-line simulation and 1,850-line renderer duplicate geometry and behavior, while event names disagree with their consumers.
assessment.codeDesign: Store movement largely clamps to bounds instead of colliding with the rendered layout. Re-entry preserves dead guards, repeated taps collapse into booleans, and physical-key lookup takes precedence over printed letters. Several store extras emit events without implementing their intended interactions.
assessment.cleanliness: Conventional TypeScript formatting and descriptive names help navigation. Duplicated store initialization, large files, loose string events, and explanatory comments attached to incomplete behavior increase maintenance risk.
assessment.completeness: Many systems exist and all 219 tests plus the typechecked build passed. However, music and speech events are disconnected, store collision and extras are simplified, and level-clear scoring awards package points again. Passing tests overstate integration coverage.

verification.browser: Title, arrival, mall and prepared store entry passed; presentation sampled

implementations.name: GPT-6 Sol
implementations.note: A recognizable, lightweight prototype. Compressed rules hide revived dead spies, loot gaps, weak collisions, and a very small sprite set.

assessment.gameDesign: The title, mall, and basic package loop are recognizable. Static sprites, simple rooms, and weak enemy behavior reduce the sense of a finished arcade game. Searching freezes store hazards, which distorts the intended risk and pacing.
assessment.architecture: Browser I/O, rendering, and seeded rules are separated, and updates clone state. Nearly all session, mall, and store rules are packed into one compressed module, with few explicit subsystem contracts.
assessment.codeDesign: A reproduced rule defect lets dead spies become active after their death timer expires. Black Friday shop generation leaves empty fixtures, guard movement ignores fixture collision, and the listening-booth geometry appears to prevent its activation. Cloning all state each tick adds unnecessary work.
assessment.cleanliness: Very long, densely compressed lines, single-letter locals, and combined responsibilities make inspection and safe changes difficult. The input module is more considered, but the overall source reads like a compressed prototype.
assessment.completeness: The basic screens and many named mechanics exist; all 25 tests and the build passed. Only six static gameplay sprites are defined, the CRT lacks real curvature, and several traversal, store, and power-up rules are partial or incorrect. The tests miss important gameplay defects.

verification.browser: Title, arrival and mall sampled; dead-spy and Black Friday defects reproduced in Node

implementations.name: Gemini 3.6 Flash
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D & WebGL CRT shader, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: Readable scaffolding, but the game loop is unfinished: stores cannot be exited, elevators do not carry the agent, and combat is incomplete.

assessment.gameDesign: The mall renders and movement can be sampled, but essential progression is blocked. Store exits are unreachable, elevator movement does not carry the player, and minimal room art offers little feedback or atmosphere.
assessment.architecture: Logic, renderer, input, and synthesis are in separate modules. The boundary is weakened by non-seeded floating-text IDs, inconsistent private fixture data versus drawing, and incomplete integration of combat and traversal.
assessment.codeDesign: Store movement clamps the player's y position to 144 while exit requires more than 154; a browser probe reproduced the trap. Enemy bullets are created without a complete movement/collision path, and searches and fixtures lack the required collision and cancellation behavior.
assessment.cleanliness: Conventional formatting and recognizable module names make the scaffolding readable. Loose contracts, hardcoded room drawing, and unused or disconnected behavior obscure what actually works.
assessment.completeness: All 14 tests and the typechecked build passed, but essential traversal and combat, guards, many NPCs/extras, and distinct store experiences are missing or partial. The unreachable store exit prevents completing the requested package loop.

verification.browser: Title and mall sampled; prepared store exit stayed blocked at y=144

implementations.name: Claude Haiku 4.5
implementations.note: The browser never leaves frame zero. Readable pieces exist, but broken timing, disconnected elevators, and instant searches prevent play.

assessment.gameDesign: Normal launch stays on the first splash frame, including after Enter, so there is no usable player experience. Direct rule calls expose basic movement, but the store and traversal systems do not support the intended loop.
assessment.architecture: Modules suggest useful separation, but rules directly invoke audio, use unseeded randomness, and attach ad hoc store state. Elevator and power-up modules are not reliably integrated, and duplicate state fields disagree.
assessment.codeDesign: The main loop resets its timestamp whenever frame is zero, producing zero elapsed time forever. Elevator updates are not called by mall rules, store movement advances a tile per frame, and searches reveal contents immediately instead of running the specified timed interaction.
assessment.cleanliness: Formatting and straightforward names are readable. Placeholder comments, disconnected code, casts to any, and extensive TypeScript errors show that the pieces were not brought to a consistent finished state.
assessment.completeness: The 13 unit tests and Vite build passed, but a separate TypeScript check failed. The browser is stuck at frame zero; guards, collision, progression, and multiple extras are absent or incomplete. The existing tests exercise isolated rules and miss the broken entry point.

verification.build: Vite build passes; separate TypeScript check fails
verification.browser: Splash remained at frame zero before and after Enter

implementations.name: Claude Haiku 5.5
implementations.technology: TypeScript + Vite, Canvas 2D with a row-based CRT effect, Web Audio synth
implementations.note: A complete, playable caper with clean rule boundaries. Power-ups never expire, the map breaks stores, and Game Over hides behind shutters.

assessment.gameDesign: The whole loop plays: zip-line arrival, elevators and escalators, timed searches with a progress bar, banners and popups, first-visit lines, level clear and harder loops, with telegraphed shots, store grace and respawn invulnerability for fairness. Opening the map inside a store leaves the room frozen on screen while the mall rules keep moving the agent, the wet-floor slide applies on every floor and can block the getaway wagon, timed power-ups never run out, and the Game Over screen ends fully covered by its shutters. Dark backdrops, abstract window displays and overflowing two-line signs make the mall less readable than the strongest entries.
assessment.architecture: Pure, seeded rules in core, mall and store modules emit typed events that a state-reading renderer and an audio layer consume; the input mapper and the splash are standalone and the browser shell is thin. The roughly 1,450-line mall module concentrates most behaviour, the game never ticks the power-up timers it owns, the map screen ignores which screen opened it, and banners persist across scene changes. Debug mode pauses real time, so the hooks cannot observe live play.
assessment.codeDesign: The elevator state machine, printed-letter input with exact key release and a tap queue, tile collision with corner assist, and once-per-volley dodge rolls are well modelled. The wet-floor check ignores floors, closing the map inside a store returns to the mall with the room still attached, timed power-ups last until death, the shutter animation covers the Game Over text, and the room system is fixed at 16 by 11 tiles without a camera.
assessment.cleanliness: Strict TypeScript with no escape hatches, short focused modules outside the mall world, readable names, and comments that explain gameplay decisions. Copy is duplicated inside rule modules despite the stated single-source rule, several sound effects, the shake output and some copy constants are defined but never used, and the README contradicts itself about the browser playtest.
assessment.completeness: Nearly every screen, mall fixture, store extra, power-up, song slot and debug option from the brief is present, with 115 tests across the listed rule areas; the strict build and the published sub-path deployment work, and browser checks logged no console errors. Real-time play covered splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, the map, pause and the CRT and mute toggles; stepped checks covered store entry, a package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over. The unticked power-up timers, the map inside stores, the floor-blind wet patch and the hidden Game Over text are working-coverage gaps; the room camera, photo strip and automatic-car ride are simplified.

verification.browser: Real-time splash, title, arrival, walking, elevator boarding, map, pause and toggles passed; prepared store entry, package search, an elevator ride to the parking level, level clear, continue and game over stepped; map-in-store, wet-floor and shutter defects reproduced

evidence.label: Map screen returns to the mall
